skills.name: Expense and revenue accounts; opening, balancing and closing accounts

note.text:
Expense (charge) accounts record costs: purchases of goods, rent, salaries, electricity, transport. Expenses are debited (they reduce the owner's equity).
Revenue (income) accounts record earnings: sales, commission received, rent received. Revenues are credited (they increase the owner's equity).
Opening an account: write its name and the opening balance on the correct side.
Balancing an account: add each side; the difference is the balance. Write it on the smaller side as “balance c/d” so both totals are equal, then bring it down on the other side as “balance b/d”.
• Debits greater than credits: a debit balance (normal for assets and expenses).
• Credits greater than debits: a credit balance (normal for liabilities, capital and revenues).
Closing: at the end of the period, expense and revenue accounts are closed (transferred to the result).

worked_example.problem: A Cash account has debits of {d1} and {d2} and credits of {c1} and {c2} FCFA. Balance it.
steps: Debit total: {d1} + {d2} = {d1 + d2}. Credit total: {c1} + {c2} = {c1 + c2}.
Balance: {d1 + d2} − {c1 + c2} = {d1 + d2 - c1 - c2}, a debit balance.
Write {d1 + d2 - c1 - c2} as balance c/d on the credit side, so both totals are {d1 + d2}; bring it down on the debit side.
worked_example.answer: Debit balance of {d1 + d2 - c1 - c2} FCFA

cards.idea: Expenses are debited; revenues are credited.
The balance is the difference between the two sides.
If debits are bigger, it is a debit balance; if credits are bigger, a credit balance.
example: Assets and expenses usually have debit balances.

check.prompt: An account has debits totalling {d} FCFA and credits totalling {c} FCFA. What kind of balance does it have?

misconceptions.explain: The balance is on the side with the bigger total.

solution: The bigger side is the {d > c ? 'debit' : 'credit'} side.
So it has {answer} of {abs(d - c)} FCFA.
